implementation_notes: On the JVM Kotlin uses java.lang.reflect.Proxy and InvocationHandler unchanged, and the API-interface client pattern (Retrofit style) is exactly this: the interface is the contract and the proxy answers every call from one handler. It is the only Kotlin realization that intercepts calls of an interface chosen at run time, but it exists only on the JVM - Kotlin/Native and Kotlin/JS have no runtime code generation.
code_sketch:
val service = Proxy.newProxyInstance(
    Service::class.java.classLoader,
    arrayOf(Service::class.java),
) { _, method, args -> method.invoke(target, *(args ?: emptyArray())) } as Service
pitfalls: The JDK mechanism is JVM-only, so common code in a multiplatform project needs an expect/actual declaration plus a generated or hand-written proxy per target.
Reflection through InvocationHandler is slower than a direct call and the handler receives boxed arguments, so wrapping a hot interface this way is measurable.

variants.name: compile-time interface delegation with overrides
variants.idiom_name: class Impl(target: Service) : Service by target
variants.implementation_notes: The language-level answer to most proxying needs: `by` makes the compiler generate forwarding members for every interface member, and overriding one of them turns that method into the interception point. It needs no reflection, cannot fail at run time and works on every Kotlin target, but it is fixed at compile time: it cannot see members the interface does not declare, and it cannot answer names the caller invents.
pitfalls: Delegation only forwards interface members, and calls the delegate makes on itself are not intercepted, so internal calls bypass the override.
Overridden members are not visible to the delegate: the delegate's own implementation of the same method still runs its own code path.
The implicit delegate property cannot be referenced, so anything the override needs must be held in a named constructor property.
